$comment: SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH for every design token. Stack-agnostic on purpose: `tool/generate-tokens.ts` renders it into a Tailwind v4 @theme stylesheet AND TypeScript consts for React Native. Never hand-edit a generated file — edit this and regenerate. Every token carries a `description`, which becomes the doc comment on the generated TypeScript member.

palette.$comment: Raw brand primitives. UI code must NOT read these directly — go through the semantic layer below so re-branding stays a one-file change. Placeholder professional-legal palette (brand not yet finalized — see O4): deep navy 'ink' for trust, warm brass for accent, paper neutrals. A `*Bright` sibling (brassBright, successBright, dangerBright) exists ONLY because its base value cannot carry text on the dark canvas at 4.5:1 — a mid-lightness hue that clears WCAG AA on paper will not clear it on inkDeep, so any new semantic colour needs its dark alias measured, not assumed.

inkBright.description: Deep navy, one step lighter — hover/pressed on ink surfaces.

inkDeep.description: Deep navy, near-black — the dark-mode canvas.

brassBright.description: Warm brass, lifted for legibility on dark surfaces.

paper.description: Neutral — warm off-white "paper"; the light-mode canvas.

linen.description: Neutral — one step down from paper, for inset/alt surfaces.

graphite.description: Neutral — near-black body text on light surfaces.

gray4.description: Neutral 4, light — hovered UI element background.

grayDark4.description: Neutral 4, dark — hovered UI element background.

gray5.description: Neutral 5, light — active / selected UI element background.

grayDark5.description: Neutral 5, dark — active / selected UI element background.

gray6.description: Neutral 6, light — subtle border and separator.

grayDark6.description: Neutral 6, dark — subtle border and separator.

gray7.description: Neutral 7, light — UI element border and focus ring.

grayDark7.description: Neutral 7, dark — UI element border and focus ring.

gray8.description: Neutral 8, light — hovered UI element border.

grayDark8.description: Neutral 8, dark — hovered UI element border.

successBright.description: Success, lifted for legibility on dark surfaces.

dangerBright.description: Danger, lifted for legibility on dark surfaces.

whiteAlpha20.description: White at 20% — hairline rules on dark surfaces.

whiteAlpha30.description: White at 30% — the pressed state of a control drawn over media.

whiteAlpha70.description: White at 70% — de-emphasized text and glyphs over media.

spacing.$comment: A 4pt base grid. Use these instead of magic numbers so layout rhythm stays consistent across every surface.

radii.$comment: Corner-radius scale for surfaces and controls. `value` is in density-independent pixels, the unit React Native's `borderRadius` speaks; `css` is the authored rem/px equivalent.

none.description: 0 — square corners, named so a component can ask for "no radius" in the same vocabulary as every other step.

xs.description: 2 — the faintest softening; checkbox ticks, tags, dense table cells.

md.description: 10 — buttons and the default control radius.

shadows.$comment: CSS-only. React Native's shadow model is per-platform, so elevation is not worth a shared token yet.

sm.description: Hairline lift — hovered rows, sticky headers.

motion.$comment: Motion primitives, so a transition duration or curve is a token rather than a number typed into a component. `value` is what React Native consumes — milliseconds as a number, easing as a string; `css` is the authored CSS equivalent; `cssVar` names the custom property outright because the Tailwind v4 theme namespace that turns a value into a real utility is NOT derivable from the token's name. Measured against the installed Tailwind (4.3.3, dist/lib.mjs): the `duration-*` utility resolves theme keys under `--transition-duration-*` (there is no `--duration-*` namespace), and `ease-*` resolves `--ease-*`. So `--transition-duration-fast` generates `duration-fast` and `--ease-standard` generates `ease-standard`. Neither namespace carries a default key of these names in Tailwind's own theme, so nothing built-in is redefined.

durationFast.description: 120ms — state flips the eye should not have to wait for: hover, focus ring, checkbox tick.

durationBase.description: 200ms — the default transition: things that move, open, or fade.

easingStandard.description: The one standard curve — quick to leave, slow to settle. Authored in the CSS form; a native consumer feeds the same four control points to Easing.bezier.

fonts.$comment: Type families as authored, for the web surfaces. React Native resolves a single registered family rather than a stack, so the native leaves map a role onto each platform's own family instead of taking this string literally — see design-system/src/lib/native-typography.native.ts, which owns that mapping for HEADING and is where MONO needs the same treatment (iOS has Menlo; Android maps the `monospace` generic). The body role needs no mapping: this stack already resolves to the platform UI family everywhere. No role ships a font file; registering one is the consuming app's job. `mono` is deliberately the same stack Tailwind's own default `--font-mono` carries, so emitting it re-declares the `font-mono` utility without changing what it means — while also giving the role a name the React Native output can carry.

heading.description: Display/heading family — apps may override to brand themselves.

body.description: Body/UI family — apps may override to brand themselves.

mono.value: ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, "Liberation Mono", "Courier New", monospace
mono.description: Monospace family — code, IDs, keyboard shortcuts, anything that must align by column.

semantic.$comment: The indirection layer. Consumers brand themselves by overriding SEMANTIC tokens, never raw palette names. Each entry resolves a `{palette.*}` alias per theme; `light` is the @theme default and `dark` is emitted under [data-theme='dark'].

card.description: Raised surface behind cards, sheets, and dialogs.

surfaceAlt.description: Inset/alternate surface — table stripes, wells, code blocks.

brand.description: The brand ink used by headers and the wordmark.

primary.description: Primary action color (filled CTAs, focus, selection).

primaryText.description: Text/icon color that sits on top of [primary].

accent.description: Warm brass accent (highlights, focus, key CTAs).

success.description: Success/confirmed state. The dark scheme lifts to a brighter green: the light value scored 3.5:1 on the dark canvas, below the 4.5:1 WCAG AA floor for body text.

danger.description: Error/destructive state. The dark scheme lifts to a brighter red: the light value scored 2.9:1 on the dark canvas, below the 4.5:1 WCAG AA floor for body text — and Field.Error renders in it.

dangerText.description: Text/icon color that sits on top of [danger]. Measured against this file's own values: 6.1:1 light (white on #B3352E) and 6.2:1 dark (#071B31 on #E27F79), both clear of the 4.5:1 WCAG AA floor for body text, so a destructive button may carry a LABEL and not only a glyph. The values are [primaryText]'s, which is what IconButton's danger glyph already rode on — this role exists so that stays true by definition rather than by coincidence, and so a brand can move the foreground on its danger fill without dragging its primary fill's along. Note the row this replaces: a hard-coded white fails at 2.8:1 on the dark scheme's lifted red, which is why the foreground has to flip with the scheme.

semantic.$comment2: THE OVERLAY ROLES BELOW DECLARE THE SAME VALUE IN BOTH SCHEMES, AND THAT IS THE POINT. Every other role answers "what does this look like on OUR canvas", and flips because the canvas does. These answer "what does this look like on a photograph" — and a photograph is not the app's canvas, does not follow the OS colour scheme, and is the one surface a component cannot see. Chrome over media is light-on-dark in a light app exactly as it is in a dark one, which is what every video player and photo viewer already does; mapping these onto the per-scheme neutral ramp would put dark glyphs on a dark scrim the moment the app was in light mode, and only on top of pictures, which is close to the hardest failure to notice. Overriding one is exactly like overriding any other role — a brand that wants warm chrome sets it once and gets it in both schemes.

overlayInk.description: Primary text/icon color for controls drawn OVER media — a player transport, a delete affordance on a frame, a filmstrip arrow. 21:1 on [overlayScrim], and 17.4:1 with that scrim at 80% over mid-grey media. Same value in both schemes; see the note above.

overlayMuted.description: De-emphasized text/icons over media — a timecode, a duration badge. 9.9:1 on [overlayScrim], 9.0:1 with that scrim at 80% over mid-grey media. Same value in both schemes.

overlayScrim.description: The darkening laid UNDER overlay controls so they are legible on media the app cannot see. Opaque on purpose: a caller applies the alpha it wants at the call site (`bg-overlay-scrim/80`, a gradient stop), because how much scrim a control needs is a property of that control, not of the theme. Same value in both schemes.

overlayHover.description: Hover fill for a control over media. An ALPHA white rather than a solid, because it composes over a frame this package has never seen — a solid would assume a background and paint a grey box on a bright photograph. Same value in both schemes.

overlayActive.description: Pressed fill for a control over media — one step up from [overlayHover], and alpha for the same reason. Same value in both schemes.

semanticDerived.$comment: Hover/active states derived from a semantic token rather than pinned to a palette value, so overriding the semantic also moves its states. CSS emits `color-mix(in srgb, ...)`; the TypeScript output pre-computes the identical sRGB blend at generation time.

ramps.$comment: A 12-step neutral ramp and its 12-step alpha twin, modelled on Radix Colors' gray/grayA (values verbatim, so a step means here exactly what its documentation says it means: 1-2 backgrounds, 3-5 component fills, 6-8 borders, 9-10 solids, 11-12 text). This is a RAMP, not the brand: the existing bg/card/surfaceAlt/line/ink roles are untouched and still resolve through `palette`, so adding this changed no consumer's default appearance. It earns its own group rather than living in `palette` because `palette` is emitted nowhere by design, and these steps have to reach both outputs; and rather than living in `semantic` because a step is a rung on a scale, not a role — `neutral9` does not say what it is for the way `danger` does. The alpha twin exists for anything that must sit over an unknown surface (an overlay, a hovered row inside a card): a solid step assumes the background it was measured against, an alpha step composes over whatever is actually there. `cssVar` names the custom property outright because kebab-casing `neutralA1` cannot produce `--color-neutral-a1`; the generator checks every one starts `--color-`. Both schemes carry all 24, and a consumer overrides a step exactly like any other colour.

neutral7.description: Neutral 7 — UI element border and focus ring.

neutralA1.description: Neutral alpha 1 — app background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA2.description: Neutral alpha 2 — subtle background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA3.description: Neutral alpha 3 — UI element background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA4.description: Neutral alpha 4 — hovered UI element background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA5.description: Neutral alpha 5 — active/selected UI element background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA6.description: Neutral alpha 6 — subtle border and separator, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA7.description: Neutral alpha 7 — UI element border and focus ring, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA8.description: Neutral alpha 8 — hovered UI element border, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA9.description: Neutral alpha 9 — solid background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA10.description: Neutral alpha 10 — hovered solid background, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA11.description: Neutral alpha 11 — low-contrast text, as a transparent overlay.

neutralA12.description: Neutral alpha 12 — high-contrast text, as a transparent overlay.
